props.title: Taste the Blood of Dracula

sections.content: Taste the Blood of Dracula marks a pivotal moment in Hammer Horror's vampire series, with Christopher Lee returning as the iconic Count. The film cleverly subverts expectations by keeping Dracula largely in the shadows while focusing on Victorian moral hypocrisy. Three wealthy businessmen seeking thrills get more than they bargained for when their debauchery leads to Dracula's resurrection. Like Dracula Has Risen from the Grave (1968), it maintains Hammer's signature gothic atmosphere but adds sharper social commentary.

sections.content: The film's strongest element is its exploration of generational conflict and Victorian repression. Director Peter Sasdy, who also helmed Countess Dracula (1971), crafts tense scenes between the supposedly respectable fathers and their rebellious children. The violence feels more brutal than in earlier Hammer films, reflecting the changing standards of 1970s horror cinema like The Exorcist (1973) and The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974). SUBHEAD: Hammer Horror's Evolution

By 1970, Hammer was adapting to compete with more explicit American horror. While maintaining period settings and gothic romance, films like Twins of Evil (1971) and Vampire Circus (1972) pushed boundaries with increased gore and sexual content. Taste the Blood of Dracula bridges this transition, keeping one foot in classic Hammer style while stepping toward modern horror sensibilities.
